title: The $40 trillion national debt is growing while Social Security goes broke—because wealthy Boomers are collecting over $100k in benefits per year
author: Joshua Hong
description: Boomers are getting 265% returns from Social Security—and the “great wealth transfer” won’t save Gen Z.
content: The United States is entering the most expensive phase of retirement. Some of America’s oldest are eligible for more than $100,000 a year in combined Social Security benefits, while remaining as one of the wealthiest generations in the country. The national debt is rising—just passing $40 trillion this month—and Social Security is set to enter insolvency by 2032, meaning it may already be too late for the generations left behind. The Congressional Budget Office projected in 2023 federal spending on Social Security and medicare will account for 81% of the increase in mandatory spending between 2023 and 2033. In 2026 alone, increases in Social Security and Medicare spending account for nearly half the projected $362 billion increase in mandatory outlays. Interest on the debt is adding even another layer on the stack of debt pancakes. CBO projects net federal interest costs will exceed $1 trillion in 2026 and rise to $2.1 trillion by 2036. That means the government is spending money to simply service the debt accumulated from previous deficits, even as entitlement programs continue growing. The state of Social Security appears to have contributed to drastically different generational outlooks on the benefit. A December 2025 survey by the Cato Institute found that only 34% of Gen Z respondents expected Social Security to exist when they reached retirement. Cato’s June 2026 analysis also found that 79% of younger respondents expected some type of cut to their own future benefits. “The survey revealed that young Americans are the least likely to expect Social Security will exist for them,” the study noted, “the most open to reforms, and the least likely to understand how the program works.” Social Security is a pay-as-you-go program , meaning most payroll taxes collected from today’s workers are used to pay benefits to today’s beneficiaries. In simpler terms, a part of your paycheck subsidizes a boomer’s benefits—and according to the Cato Institute’s 2025 polling, only 45% of Americans correctly understand how the program works. Under current law, employees and employers each pay 6.2% of wages into Social Security up to an annual taxable maximum, which is $184,500 in 2026. Self-employed workers pay the combined 12.4% rate. That structure worked far smoother when there were many workers for every retiree. But the demographic math changed—baby boomers are now moving through retirement while younger generations deal with record job market difficulty. And it doesn’t help that Social Security beneficiaries are getting over double their investment into the program back. A median-wage worker retiring in 2027 is expected to receive roughly $730,000 in lifetime Social Security benefits compared with less than $200,000 in combined contributions from the worker and employer. When the employer contribution is excluded, the lifetime benefits amount to roughly 265% of what the worker personally paid into Social Security. The current system is effectively relying on the workers of today—which include millennials and the younger end of Gen X—to finance retirees. What the government is going to do about it The federal government has reached a point where arithmetic becomes unavoidable. The 2026 Social Security trustees report projects that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund will be depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032. At that point, continuing program income would cover only 78% of scheduled retirement benefits. The theoretically combined Social Security trust funds are projected to be depleted in 2034, when incoming revenue would cover 83% of scheduled benefits. Without congressional action, that would mean an automatic reduction in benefits. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates the retirement program would face an approximately 22% across-the-board reduction when the retirement trust fund is exhausted. The committee has proposed one way to address the issue—putting a ceiling on the benefits paid to its wealthiest retirees. Dubbed the “Six Figure Limit,” the proposal would cap Social Security benefits at $100,000 annually for a married couple retiring at the normal retirement age, with the limit adjusted for marital status and claiming age. A single retiree’s comparable limit would be $50,000. The proposal is aimed at an extremely small group. CRFB estimates the cap would only really affect the top 0.05% of couples in its early years, households with average annual retirement income above $2.5 million and average net worth above $65 million. The organization says the cap would become more consequential over time as Social Security’s maximum benefits continue to rise. CBS News reported in March that roughly one million individual Social Security beneficiaries receive at least $50,000 a year, meaning a married couple with two such beneficiaries could receive more than six-figures. The Social Security Administration did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune . Boomers are rich—but no one else will get their wealth Baby boomers collectively hold roughly $93 trillion in wealth, according to Visa Business and Economic Insights, but only about $36 trillion is expected to pass to millennials and Gen X over the next two decades. The difference is reflected in taxes, debt, spending during retirement and the concentration of wealth among the richest boomers. After the dedication in liabilities, about $88 trillion remain—and the top 1% holds about one-third of that wealth. Boomers are also expected to spend approximately $16 trillion during retirement on housing, food, healthcare, prescriptions and other expenses. That means the “Great Wealth Transfer” will not move a $93 trillion pile of assets from retirees to younger Americans. A substantial portion of it will never be inherited, and much of what is transferred will be concentrated among the affluent households. But the Social Security program was created as social insurance, not as a means-tested welfare program. So someone who earned more during their career generally receives a larger benefit, subject to the program’s formula and taxable maximum. An affluent retiree can qualify for a fat Social Security check even when that benefit represents only a small portion of their overall income. According to the Cato Institute, Social Security should focus more heavily on protecting seniors from poverty while giving younger workers greater opportunity to build private retirement savings. Their analysis points to systems in other developed countries across the world that use combinations of basic pensions, targeted benefits, automatic adjustments and private savings mechanisms. The United States’ earnings-related benefit structure can produce increasingly generous payments for higher earners, based on the Cato Institute’s report. The organization notes that a maximum-earning worker claiming Social Security at age 70 can receive more than $61,000 a year, while arguing policymakers could reduce benefits for higher-income retirees in a restructuring. “Policymakers should consider fundamentally rethinking the program’s structure and transform it into a system that ensures seniors are protected from poverty when they can no longer work,” the institute wrote, “while also freeing up resources for younger workers to save more on their own.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: In border states, even Trump’s own party wants the Canada fight to be over
author: Nick Lichtenberg
description: Governors, senators, and automakers in Maine, Vermont, and Michigan have spent 18 months warning the White House a trade war with Canada would bite.
content: When U.S.-Canada trade talks collapsed for good last Friday night , the recriminations broke out almost instantly, and not just between Washington and Ottawa. In Maine, Vermont and Michigan—three states with outsized economic exposure to Canada—elected officials from both parties and the executives who run the region’s largest employers have spent the past week saying, in various ways, the same thing: enough. The latest escalation came Monday, when U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box Canada was to blame for the breakdown, saying negotiators had reached the outline of a deal by Tuesday night only for Ottawa to add last-minute demands. “In the last hours, I think there were things that the Canadians just—you know, they wanted more,” Greer said. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has offered the mirror-image account , saying the U.S. side introduced “last-minute changes” to proposed terms that were “unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.” Politico ‘s reporting on the 72 hours before the deal cratered found the dispute came down to a central sticking point: U.S. tariff rates on heavy-duty trucks, which Canadian negotiators pushed to lower late in the process, though U.S. officials also cited internal turf wars and Carney pointed to American refusal to extend auto-tariff relief to medium- and heavy-duty trucks. The practical result was the same regardless of which account is right: 50% U.S. tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods took effect at 12:01 a.m. Aug. 22, and Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics are set to hit Sept. 8. Maine’s senators, from opposite parties, agree Maine’s congressional delegation has been unusually unified for a state represented by one Republican and one independent who caucuses with Democrats. Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican facing a competitive reelection race this fall, called the tariffs “a mistake” in an interview with News Center Maine , adding she’d recently met with Canada’s ambassador to press on dairy trade barriers and still wants “the very friendly, economically beneficial relationship” restored. On social media, Collins urged “both sides to return to the negotiating table,” writing on X the on-again/off-again trade talks between the U.S. and Canada lead to “higher costs, risk, and uncertainty for Maine businesses.” Sen. Angus King, the state’s independent senator who caucuses with Democrats, has focused on the lobster industry specifically, warning Canada’s coming 25% tariff on lobster—which takes effect alongside the broader Sept. 8 retaliation—could be compounded if Trump imposes a reciprocal charge on the processed product when it re-enters the U.S. “If the president’s misguided trade war further escalates, the processed lobsters could be taxed again when they are shipped back from Canada to the United States,” King said , noting almost half of Maine’s fall lobster catch goes to Canada for processing. Collins raised the same underlying vulnerability months earlier in a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing , telling Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick Maine’s meat, blueberries, potatoes, lobster, and lumber are largely processed across the border—testimony Lutnick answered by pointing to USMCA rules governing which goods qualify for tariff-free treatment. Vermont’s governor: consistent from the start Vermont Gov. Phil Scott, a Republican, has been arguably Trump’s most consistent GOP critic on this specific issue, repeating a version of the same warning through every phase of the standoff. In July, Scott said flatly : “My feelings on punitive tariffs imposed on Canada have not changed over the last two years and are simply a bad idea that will lead to increased costs on Vermonters.” When the administration briefly paused the tariffs in mid-August, Scott called it a hopeful sign , while noting Vermont still had “a long ways to go to rebuild this relationship with our friends in the north.” When the pause lapsed and the tariffs took effect anyway, Scott’s tone hardened further: “The Trump tariffs are basically taxes—they raise costs for families, farmers and employers on both sides of the border and strain a relationship that has made both countries stronger and more secure,” he said in a statement in late August . Vermont’s exposure explains the persistence: Canada is Vermont’s largest export market by a wide margin, accounting for 31% of the state’s total goods exports in 2025—more than double its next-largest market, according to the U.S. Trade Representative . Michigan’s governor and the Big Three close ranks No governor has been louder than Michigan’s Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat who has criticized the tariffs since shortly after they were first imposed in February 2025 and escalated her rhetoric as the fight dragged on for roughly a year and a half. “It is a blunt tool. You can’t just pull out the tariff hammer to swing at every problem without a clear defined end-goal,” Whitmer said in an April 2025 speech , warning tariffs risked economic “paralysis.” In an October 2025 keynote address delivered in Canada, Whitmer said tariffs put 1.2 million Michigan jobs at risk, citing the additional 25% tariff already in place on foreign-made auto parts. Whitmer renewed the attack this week after talks collapsed, posting on X. on Aug. 22 Michigan residents were “uniquely impacted by DC Republicans’ ongoing, chaotic tariff wars with Canada,” and that the tariffs amounted to “a tax hike on Michigan families and businesses by raising prices at the grocery store and the gas pump.” Detroit’s automakers have made the same case largely through industry channels and public disclosures. Canada has toughened its own countermeasures against U.S.-based automakers that scaled back Canadian production, cutting the tariff-free import quota for Stellantis by 50% and for GM by 24.2%. Trump has since announced a 50% U.S. tariff on Canadian vehicles, trucks, auto parts and steel set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027—an escalation from the current 25% rate. Ford and General Motors declined to comment on the situation when contacted by Fortune . Carney, for his part, used remarks this weekend to frame the moment in starker terms than any previous point in the dispute, saying the country was “ at war ” with the U.S. economically. Greer has continued to defend the administration’s account publicly, saying Canada introduced new demands and walked back other commitments in the final hours before the deal collapsed. The through line connecting Augusta, Montpelier, and Lansing is none of this was requested by the states most exposed to it—and officials in all three, across party lines, have been saying so since the fight began. What’s changed is the tone. Collins, Scott, and Whitmer spent much of the past year and a half framing their objections as cautionary. This week, after a second round of tariffs actually took effect and a retaliation date is locked in for Sept. 8, all three sounded less like they were warning of a risk and more like they were describing a loss already sustained. title: Bitcoin is having a great month—but Solana is doing even better as coin soars above $100
author: Camila Grigera Naón
description: Investors have found fresh reasons to buy Solana beyond Bitcoin’s comeback.
content: Bitcoin may have broken $80,000 , but Solana is stealing the spotlight. SOL, the blockchain’s native token, climbed more than 23% over the past week, with much of that gain coming in the past 24 hours. The token recently crossed $100 for the first time since February and now trades at $107, according to crypto analytics platform CoinGecko. Solana’s price surge coincided with record-breaking trading volume in Solana exchange-traded funds. On Tuesday, Solana reported that its ETF cumulative inflows hit a record $1.2 billion, with nearly $34 million coming in on Monday alone. It marked the biggest single day so far this year, capping five straight days of inflows. The total stablecoin value on Solana approached $16 billion on Thursday, according to data aggregator DefiLlama, giving investors more readily available dollar-backed liquidity on the network. These gains have come during a more favorable stretch for crypto markets. Last week, the Treasury Department announced a series of bond buybacks, which investors interpreted as a sign that more cash could circulate through financial markets. The rebound marked a sharp reversal from the crypto downturn that began last October. When investors anticipate more liquidity, they tend to take on more risk by investing in speculative assets like crypto. Bitcoin rose first and lifted the broader market, but Solana has outperformed many other altcoins, a catchall term for tokens other than Bitcoin. “$SOL is moving upwards here, but as you can see, the bear market lasted for a year and we’ve not even gained 20% of that back. Great period upon us,” wrote crypto analyst Michael van de Poppe. Alongside its price, Solana has benefited from signs of growing network activity. Bitcoin’s appeal rests largely on its fixed supply and store-of-value narrative, while Solana’s case depends more on its ability to support fast, low-cost trading and other decentralized finance applications. According to DefiLlama, Solana’s decentralized exchanges handled nearly $56 billion in trades over the past 30 days and have processed more than $10 billion so far this week. Some of that activity came from memecoin trading , which has increased sharply in recent weeks. Solana’s low transaction costs and Pump.fun, a popular token-launch platform, have made it a popular venue for traders to quickly buy and sell such highly speculative tokens. But the volume can disappear as fast as it arrives and does not necessarily signal lasting demand. Still, the numbers do not show that investors are broadly abandoning Bitcoin for Solana. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs drew more than $232 million in net inflows on Thursday and recorded daily trading volume of $8 billion, according to crypto analytics platform CoinGlass. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Chartstopper: August 21, 2026
author: Michael Normyle
description: The bond market was the big story this week.
content: This Week The bond market was the big story this week. Long-term Treasury yields have increased in recent months, as 30-year Treasury yields recently hit their high since 2007 , facing pressure from a growing debt load (which hit $40 trillion this week), higher inflation (which we’ll get to), and competition from artificial intelligence hyperscaler bond issuance (boosting investment grade-issuance 36% year-on-year). With yields rising, Treasury Secretary Bessent announced the Treasury will “at least double” its buybacks of long-term (10- to 30-year) Treasuries to $4+ billion from September to November (these buybacks provide liquidity by buying older Treasuries). While this initially led to a drop in long-term bond yields, it’s since reversed, seemingly upon the realization that a few extra billion dollars in buybacks does little in the face of ongoing $2 trillion deficits . In terms of inflation, U.S. oil prices are up about 5% this week as there’s no end in sight for the Iran conflict. Notably, the 60-day Memorandum of Understanding expired this week without extension or even ongoing talks . Instead, Iran seized a United Arab Emirates-linked oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, there were reports Iran’s military is taking a “ fully offensive ” posture as it prepares to a return to war, and President Trump called for “unprecedented” “ economic warfare ” against Iran. Relatedly, in Walmart’s (WMT) earnings this week (beat), the company noted that “higher fuel prices” are causing “some incremental pressure on the consumer .” For the week, the Nasdaq-100® is down 2%, while 10-year Treasury yields are up a few basis points to over 4.7%.

title: Biweekly Investment Insights: AI resurgence propels equities as breadth builds
author: Yanni Angelakos
description: AI-driven earnings and broader EPS growth continue to support equities and market breadth. Softer Fed rate hike expectations are boosting risk assets, even as global bond yields remain near multi-decade highs. While markets may be volatile ahead of U.S. midterm elections, history suggests gains often follow.
content: Yanni Angelakos, Head of Investment Insights, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms Mike Cho, CFA, Senior Research Analyst, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms Tony Kristic, Senior Research Analyst, Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Strong earnings push equities to new highs amidst higher rates AI theme continues to underpin equities & earnings, broader EPS growth rates support widening market breadth Softening Fed rate hike expectations have also helped risk assets while global bond yields hover near multi-decade highs Markets historically choppy heading into U.S. November midterm elections, then advance over ensuing months Although the focus is the impact of AI on the U.S. economy and markets, the AI theme is, of course, a global phenomenon. Per our Biweekly Chart in Focus, if looking at Taiwanese exports as a proxy for global AI and technology demand, though annual growth has slowed it remains at a very healthy 39.2% on a YoY basis as of July. Nasdaq-100 and semiconductor YoY returns similarly remain at elevated levels despite having slowed as momentum cooled. From a bottom-up perspective, Q2 earnings season helped allay AI spending concerns in the near-term. However, just as importantly, earnings helped to underpin a broadening of equity returns as U.S. equities hit new highs—the median Russell 3000 EPS growth rate is 15% in Q2 YoY, the highest since Q3 2021. Also helping risk assets over the past two weeks at a macro level were softer July U.S. CPI and PPI reports which scaled back the market pricing of Federal Reserve rate hikes. As of August 17th, there is an 89% chance of a 25 basis point hike by year’s end versus at least one 25 bp hike priced in only a week earlier. While a near-term relief for markets, investors are still contending with multi-year highs in U.S. Treasury yields as the 10-year is at 4.70% and global government bond yields also remain elevated. As the markets move past Q2 earnings, summer winds down, and the calendar turns to September, based on history, we suspect that the market narrative will turn to the U.S. midterm elections in early November. Historically, per Goldman Sachs, market volatility ramps up heading into midterm elections. Yet, these elections tend to be more noise than anything as the S&P 500 typically averages a total return of 14.1% over the six months following midterm elections, since 1970, according to BlackRock. Biweekly Chart in Focus: Taiwanese exports, Nasdaq-100 Index® (Nasdaq-100®), PHLX Semiconductor™ Index YoY% have cooled but still at elevated levels Source: Bloomberg. As of August 14, 2026. Details A strong Q2 2026 earnings season winds down With only about 13% of S&P 500 market cap left to report over the last two weeks of Q2 earnings season (~8% of this being NVDA), around 90% of reporting S&P 500 companies have beaten EPS estimates, per Bloomberg. Focusing on the megacap tech space, which has helped the latest rebound in U.S. equities (Nasdaq-100 is +11% from its July 29 th lows), 89% of Nasdaq-100 companies that have reported as of August 14 th have beaten EPS estimates. The Nasdaq-100 blended (actuals + estimates) EPS growth rate now stands at approximately 76%—significantly higher than the consensus growth forecast of 29.2%. As discussed in our prior piece , while this is skewed by significant contributions from Amazon and Google due to unrealized gains in equity stakes, these are nevertheless very strong earnings trends. Stepping back, the growth rate of the median stock’s EPS in the Russell 3000 Index is 15% YoY—its highest rate since Q3 2021 which benefited from Covid-19-time frame comparisons (Figure 1). Figure 1: Russell 3000 median stock EPS YoY growth Sources: Morgan Stanley, FactSet This widening of EPS growth breadth supports the broadening of U.S. equity returns on a YTD basis (Figure 2) while also keeping equity valuations in check relative to their 10-year averages compared with the middle of 2025 (Figure 3). Figure 2: Thematic 2026 YTD U.S. equity returns Source: Bloomberg. As of August 14, 2026. Figure 3: Global equity next 12-month P/Es relative to 10-year averages Source: Bloomberg. As of August 17, 2026. Softer U.S. inflation trends yet central bank rate expectations and government 10-year yields remain elevated Softer Tier 1 U.S. economic data—July NFPs and retail sales—coupled with cooler-than-expected inflation—July CPI (core inflation was up just 2.5% year-over-year in July, the slowest since 2021) and PPI—caused markets to largely price out a September Fed rate hike. The latest data also brought down expectations for the next several Fed meetings (Figure 4). In the very near-term, the markets will be parsing global central bankers’ signaling at the upcoming Jackson Hole Symposium on August 27 th to 29 th . Figure 4: Number of 25 bp rate hikes or cuts priced in by market for major central banks Source: Bloomberg However, Treasury yields have also remained elevated as U.S. inflation remains a source of concern for the Fed (Figure 5) with oil prices hovering around $80/bbl for WTI crude since late July, Fed policy uncertainties lingering (as we showed in the decomposition of the YTD change in Treasury 10-year yields in our prior piece ), and U.S. government debt levels to climb leading to widening fiscal deficits (Figure 6). This, of course, is not only a U.S. dynamic as global bond yields are at multi-year highs (Figure 7). While market pricing of Fed rate hikes has softened, as Figure 4 also shows, the market pricing of ECB and BoJ’s rates trajectory is higher relative to the Fed as they battle inflation, energy supply shocks (more so than the U.S. which is an energy exporter), and fiscal concerns. Figure 5: U.S. inflation measures have moderated, though remain sticky Source: Bloomberg Figure 6: U.S. federal spending & revenues (% of nominal GDP) Source: Office of Management and Budget, Congressional Budget Office, Peter G. Peterson Foundation Figure 7: Global government 10-year debt yields remain elevated Source: Bloomberg Historical U.S. midterm election trends As recent U.S. elections cycles have shown, predicting outcomes can be very difficult and, though informative, polling can prove to be unreliable. What can be useful for investors is looking at history as a gauge of market reactions leading into and following midterm elections in early November. While historical averages cannot be relied upon as forecasts, Figure 8 below shows that equity volatility usually increases heading into midterm elections but then tends to fade. Figure 9 shows the total return for U.S. equities before and after midterm elections since 1970. The interesting part from Figure 9 is that S&P 500 total returns were 16.1% on average over the six months following mid-term elections in which the President’s party either gains or keeps control of both chambers of Congress. However, when the governing party has a “trifecta” and subsequently loses control of at least one of the chambers of Congress during the midterms, forward 6-month returns were almost 6% lower (10.4%). The takeaway from these charts for investors? If history is any guide, pre-midterm election volatility does not necessarily portend poor forward equity returns and timing the markets is difficult, particularly around what can be unpredictable macro-oriented events. Notes: “Lost Control” defined as scenarios in which one party was controlling the presidency and both chambers of Congress heading into midterms, then lost control of at least one of them. title: What is the Nasdaq-100? A Guide to One of the World's Most-Watched Indexes
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: At its core, the Nasdaq-100 tracks 100 of the largest non-financial Nasdaq-listed companies, as measured by the total market value of those companies’ outstanding shares.
content: The Nasdaq-100® (NDX®) is a globally recognized index of 100 of the most innovative large cap companies listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market®. Widely used as a benchmark for the technology sector as well as US large cap growth, it's one of the most tracked indexes in the world from an investable product standpoint, with more than $1.7 trillion of exposure linked to it globally as of June 30, 2026. Here's what you need to know. Quick Facts: Inception Date January 31, 1985 Number of Components 100 Weighting Method Modified market capitalization Rebalance Schedule Quarterly Reconstitution Schedule Annual (December) Top Sectors Technology, Consumer Discretionary, Healthcare Financial companies included? No Index Ticker Symbol NDX How the Nasdaq-100 Works At its core, the Nasdaq-100 tracks 100 of the largest non-financial Nasdaq-listed companies, as measured by the total market value of those companies’ outstanding shares. The index uses a modified market capitalization weighting method, which means bigger companies have more influence on the index's movements, but with guardrails in place to prevent any single company from dominating the whole index. This distinguishes it from a pure market-cap-weighted index and helps limit concentration among its top holdings. While the Nasdaq-100 has a longstanding reputation as a "tech-heavy index," its reach goes well beyond Silicon Valley. The Nasdaq-100 is home to companies that have reshaped how we live, work, shop, and connect. The index spans multiple sectors, centering on: Technology — software, semiconductors, hardware Consumer Discretionary — e-commerce, retail, media, entertainment, travel & leisure Healthcare — biotech, medical devices, pharmaceuticals Consumer Staples , Industrials , and Telecommunications Basic Materials, Energy, Utilities, Real Estate (minimal exposure) It's also worth distinguishing the Nasdaq-100 from the Nasdaq Composite® . The Composite includes every company listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market — more than 3,000 securities spanning all sizes and sectors — whereas the Nasdaq-100 is far more selective, tracking only the 100 largest non-financial companies on the exchange. And while many of those components are US-headquartered, the Nasdaq-100 is explicitly not limited to American companies. The index is open to any company listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market — regardless of where that company is based — so it includes globally recognized companies headquartered outside the United States. That international dimension is part of what makes the Nasdaq-100 a global innovation benchmark, not just an American one. Nasdaq-100 vs. S&P 500: Key Differences The Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500 are often mentioned in the same breath, but they're measuring different segments of the market. Here's how they compare: Nasdaq-100 S&P 500 Number of Companies 100 ~500 Exchange Requirement Nasdaq-listed only Any major U.S. exchange Financial Sector Included? No Yes Performance Profile Growth/Innovation-driven Broad U.S. market Sector Concentration New economy focus More balanced The S&P 500 is designed to represent the broad U.S. economy — 500 companies across all sectors, from banks to oil producers to tech giants. By contract, the Nasdaq-100, which trades under the ticker symbol NDX, by contrast, is explicitly focused on non-financial companies at the forefront of global innovation. If the S&P 500 is a snapshot of the economy, the Nasdaq-100 is more of a portrait of where innovation is happening. According to Nasdaq Global Indexes, Bloomberg, and Factset , as of year-end 2025, Nasdaq-100 companies represented slightly more than half of the total market capitalization of the S&P 500, with the average NDX company size approximately three times as large. How a Company Gets Added to the Nasdaq-100 There are specific eligibility requirements a company must meet to be included in the Nasdaq-100. To be considered for inclusion, a company must: Be listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market® or Nasdaq Global Market® tiers Be classified as a non-financial company (banks, insurance companies, and other financial firms including REITs are excluded) Meet minimum average daily trading volume requirements to ensure liquidity Have been listed on Nasdaq for a minimum seasoning period before becoming eligible The index is reconstituted annually each December, when Nasdaq reviews the full list and makes any additions or removals based on updated rankings. In addition, the index is rebalanced quarterly to keep the weighting methodology in check and ensure no single company grows disproportionately large relative to the others. Outside these scheduled events, special rebalances may occasionally take place to manage index concentration, while fast-entry rules enable intra-quarter additions for the very largest companies that conduct their IPOs or switch their listings to Nasdaq, subject to conditions. Top Sectors and Holdings The current Nasdaq-100 components reflect the index's growth-oriented DNA. Technology consistently represents the largest share of the index by weight, followed by Consumer Discretionary and Healthcare. The top holdings by weight typically include companies like Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Tesla, Meta Platforms, and Broadcom — joined by names such as Walmart and Costco. These are some of the largest and most widely held names in global equity markets, and they collectively represent a significant portion of the index's total weight, although they are limited by weight caps applied at the quarterly rebalances and the annual reconstitution. The full list of companies that comprise the Nasdaq-100, in order of their weight in the index, can be found on Nasdaq's website. How to Invest in the Nasdaq-100 Investors can't buy the Nasdaq-100 directly because it is an index, not a security, but there are several practical ways to gain exposure to it. The most popular approach is through exchange-traded funds (ETFs). The Invesco QQQ Trust ETF ( QQQ ) historically tracked the Nasdaq-100's performance, but BlackRock and State Street launched similar funds that also track the index, in July and June of 2026, respectively. Other ETF options exist as well, including leveraged and inverse variants for more sophisticated investors. Mutual funds that track the index are another option, typically accessible through retirement accounts and brokerage platforms. For a full overview of available investment vehicles, visit the Nasdaq-100 Ways to Invest page. Why the Nasdaq-100 Matters Over the long run, the Nasdaq-100 has historically delivered substantial outperformance compared to broader market benchmarks — a reflection of its concentration in high-growth sectors. On a trailing 10-year basis as of December 31, 2025, the Nasdaq-100 has generated total returns of approximately 500% vs. the S&P 500's approximately 300%. Investors can explore historical Nasdaq-100 performance data directly from Nasdaq. That said, higher growth potential also comes with higher volatility. title: Private Markets Data Expansion: What LPs and GPs Need to Know
author: Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms
description: Private market AUM now exceeds $20 trillion, but data infrastructure hasn't kept pace. Learn how institutional allocators can close the gap with modern technology.
content: Key Takeaways Private market assets under management have grown to more than $20 trillion across all capital structures , making data infrastructure a strategic priority. Manual data extraction and fragmented reporting systems can make meaningful performance benchmarking near-impossible for institutional allocators. Evolving regulatory disclosure frameworks may increase operational reporting demands that can be difficult to address efficiently through highly manual processes. Cloud-native platforms and API-driven integration enable institutional allocators to consolidate fund-level data from multiple sources into a single, searchable environment. Firms that treat data infrastructure as a strategic asset rather than a back-office function may be better positioned to benchmark performance, satisfy regulatory obligations, and make better investment decisions. While private markets represent a significant opportunity for institutional allocators, they also come with complexity and challenges. Assets under management across all private markets capital structures have grown to more than $20 trillion , but the infrastructure supporting it is not keeping pace. As they were built for smaller, simpler allocations, the operational systems used to collect, normalize, and analyze data from private markets remain mostly manual. Many organizations managing multi-billion-dollar alternative portfolios still rely on quarterly PDFs, fragmented GP portals, and spreadsheets. This has led to a widening gap between the scale of opportunities and the information available to act on them. What allocators now need is a framework to close this gap, with supporting technology and implementation steps that investment committees can take.

title: Beyond Earth: The Rise of a Commercial Space Economy
author: Salvatore Bruno, CETF®
description: Explore the rise of the commercial space economy, from satellite communications and AI-enabled data platforms to space infrastructure, and how the Nasdaq-100® provides exposure to this long-term growth theme.
content: Salvatore Bruno, CETF®, Senior Director, Head of Americas Nasdaq Index Insights Sanjana Prabhakar, Senior Specialist, Nasdaq Index Insights Key Takeaways The space economy is entering a multi-decade, infrastructure-led investment cycle, transitioning from government-led to commercially driven markets. Industry growth is supported by a combination of declining launch costs, increased commercial participation, and expanding application areas , though monetization remains uneven across segments. Advances in AI and data processing capabilities are beginning to play a more important role , enabling the extraction of value from large volumes of satellite-generated data across multiple end markets. Government spending and geopolitical considerations continue to provide a structural demand base , particularly in areas such as secure communications, defense, and surveillance infrastructure. While longer-duration opportunities—including space exploration, human spaceflight, and resource extraction— offer potential for future growth, they remain at an early stage and are subject to technological, regulatory, and economic uncertainties. The Nasdaq-100 provides exposure to the space economy through companies that supply the semiconductors, cloud infrastructure, AI capabilities, communications technologies, and data platforms that increasingly underpin space-based applications. Within the Nasdaq-100, participation in the space economy is distributed across multiple layers of the value chain. Rocket Lab may be viewed as the "picks-and-shovels" layer of the space economy , supplying critical infrastructure for launch, satellite deployment, and in-orbit operations. Qualcomm may be viewed as the enabling technology layer , helping connect satellites, devices, and networks through advanced communications hardware and standards development. Industry size is projected to expand from ~$630B (2023) to ~$1.8T by 2035 (~9% CAGR) , outpacing global GDP growth 1 . The space economy and its fundamental underpinnings Investor enthusiasm for the space economy has reached a cyclical high, catalyzed by SpaceX’s IPO at a valuation of over $1.75 trillion—one of the largest public offerings in history 2 . SpaceX marked its debut in the Nasdaq-100® through a “fast entry” rule that allows massive IPOs that meet certain criteria to be eligible to enter the index after 15 trading days. As of July 16, 2026, it ranks as the 8th largest company in the Nasdaq-100 by market cap at $1.8 trillion, slotting in between Broadcom and Meta. However, the company’s index weight is tied to its $106 billion float-adjusted market cap, not its $1.8 trillion headline number. At $106 billion float-adjusted, SpaceX ranks far lower in the NDX® weight hierarchy, comparable in float-adjusted terms to names like Palo Alto Networks, ranking just outside the 20 th largest index weights. SpaceX has officially launched more satellites into orbit than all other companies, governments, and organizations combined in the entire history of spaceflight. It achieved its unprecedented lead by rapidly building and deploying the Starlink mega-constellation. It has launched a cumulative total of 15,262 satellites, recently crossing the threshold to surpass the 15,138 satellites launched by every other entity in human history combined (since 1957). While the rest of the world's total represents nearly seven decades of spaceflight, SpaceX accomplished the majority of its massive deployment in just the last six years 3 . Despite the surge in interest from investors, the space economy remains in the early stages of a multi-decade infrastructure build-out, with capital increasingly directed toward foundational layers such as launch, satellite constellations, and orbital services. The sector’s momentum has been reflected in public equities, with shares of commercial space companies—including Nasdaq-listed Rocket Lab and AST SpaceMobile—delivering outsized gains over the past year. At the same time, comparisons to prior speculative cycles have emerged, underscoring rising valuation risk as capital runs ahead of realized earnings. Structurally, the industry is undergoing a transition analogous to the commercialization of the internet in the 1990s—shifting from a government funded endeavor to a commercial market. This evolution is expanding the addressable opportunity set beyond traditional aerospace into a broad range of applications, spanning launch services, satellite infrastructure, connectivity, Earth observation, defense, and emerging areas such as in-space manufacturing and resource utilization. From a sizing perspective, the global space economy generated approximately $630 billion in revenue in 2023 and is projected to reach $1.8 trillion by 2035, implying roughly 9% annualized growth—well above expected global GDP growth 4 . The investment case is often associated with a convergence of structural demand (government mandates, defense modernization), cost deflation (reusable launch), and expanding commercial applications — with the SpaceX IPO serving as a potential near-term catalyst for the broader sector. Near-term revenue is concentrated in scalable, commercially viable segments , particularly satellite connectivity, positioning/navigation/timing (PNT), and Earth observation, which are driving the majority of current industry growth. Cost declines—driven by reusable launch technologies—are lowering potential barriers to entry , accelerating private-sector participation and increasing deployment activity across the value chain. AI integration is emerging as a critical monetization layer , transforming satellite infrastructure into data-driven platforms and enabling new service-based revenue models. Geopolitical dynamics and defense spending are reinforcing demand , particularly for sovereign communication systems, tracking capabilities, and space-based infrastructure. Longer-duration opportunities—including human spaceflight, in-space manufacturing, and resource utilization—offer significant optionality , but remain early-stage with execution, regulatory, and economic uncertainties. Within the Nasdaq-100, participation in the space economy is distributed across multiple layers of the value chain. While companies like Rocket Lab (a recent NDX addition) represent direct infrastructure exposure, others such as Qualcomm provide enabling technologies—particularly in satellite communications—underscoring the index’s indirect but meaningful exposure to the theme. Qualcomm's space economy participation is primarily centered on enabling satellite-to-smartphone connectivity (D2D), automotive satellite integration, and positioning its chipsets as the underlying silicon for next-generation satellite communication standards. However, these efforts remain a relatively modest component of the company’s broader diversified strategy. Innovations like the Snapdragon X105 5G Modem-RF support both narrowband (messaging) and broadband satellite connectivity without replacing the device 5 . In parallel, Qualcomm has pursued targeted partnerships to advance satellite-enabled use cases. The company has worked alongside Ericsson and Thales Alenia Space to successfully test 5G satellite calls, demonstrating the viability of integrating low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite channels with terrestrial core networks 6 . From an intellectual property perspective, Qualcomm’s positioning is particularly notable. The company has filed roughly 1/6th of all patents within spacecraft and satellite-related technologies in the past few years, per Nasdaq’s analysis of IFI CLAIMS data—underscoring its role in shaping the standards layer of the emerging space communications ecosystem. Rocket Lab positions itself as a fully integrated space company, offering launch services, spacecraft design, component manufacturing, and on-orbit management — making space access more efficient and affordable. The company manufactures spacecraft components, solar arrays, and flight software, and has even acquired robotics leaders like Motiv Space Systems to build Mars-proven technology 7 . It is expanding into medium-lift capacity with their carbon-composite Neutron rocket, which is built for constellation deployments and exploration missions 8 . It is manufacturing 18 satellites for the U.S. Space Development Agency's (SDA) Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture (PWSA) Tracking Layer Tranche 3 program, bringing cumulative SDA awards to over $1.3 billion 9 . Satellite Technology: Unlocking Trillion-Dollar Addressable Markets The investment case for the space economy is increasingly anchored in the rise of satellite communications, positioning/navigation/timing (PNT), and Earth observation as core growth engines, enabling global connectivity and entirely new business models across industries. As satellite technology matures and integrates more deeply with digital systems, it is potentially unlocking trillion-dollar addressable markets. This momentum is reinforced by a surge of deployment activity, with nearly 43,000 satellites forecast to launch over the next decade, representing a total market value of ~$655 billion, with an average of 3,700 launches per year driven primarily by four commercial next-generation satellite orbit (NGSO) mega-constellations 10 . This shift is further amplified by geopolitical dynamics, which are driving sustained demand for sovereign, secure communication infrastructure. Layered on top of these trends is the integration of AI with satellite infrastructure, enabling global, real-time connectivity. Looking ahead, advancements in launch capabilities such as SpaceX’s planned deployment of larger Starlink satellites using its Starship rocket, are expected to further expand constellation capacity. There are ~30,000+ tracked objects in Earth orbit, of which roughly half are active satellites (~16,000), leaving a substantial share as non-functional debris. Collisions between defunct satellites and debris can generate thousands of new high-velocity fragments, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of fragmentation. In a worst-case scenario—often referred to as the Kessler Syndrome—this cascade effect could render entire orbital zones increasingly hazardous or even unusable 11 . As the industry evolves, the market is bifurcating between small, mass-market constellations and large, specialized platforms, with the latter capturing a larger share of industry value. While established aerospace companies and government agencies remain significant players, new entrants such as SpaceX and Blue Origin are reshaping competitive dynamics and traditional business models. At the same time, advanced AI/ML capabilities are expected to be an important near-term driver for converting massive satellite constellation data volumes into near-instantaneous, actionable insights for agriculture, finance, forestry, and government. As data becomes the primary asset, military satellite programs are evolving from asset ownership toward subscription-based data and services models [12] .Ultimately, satellite technology is evolving from a capacity-driven infrastructure buildout into a data-centric ecosystem, where long-term value is determined by the ability to monetize information rather than simply deploy assets in orbit. Satellite Technology: From Infrastructure Buildout to Data Monetization Space Exploration: Catalyst for Dual-Use Technology Space exploration missions have historically been a powerful catalyst for dual-use technology, with advances in propulsion, materials science, robotics, AI navigation, and life support systems translating into broad commercial applications 13 . In this context, the U.S. is increasingly relying on private sector innovation to reduce mission costs, with dual-use technology becoming central for both defense and civilian exploration missions 14 . Recent progress in propulsion technologies, particularly nuclear thermal propulsion (NTP) and solar electric propulsion (SEP), are dramatically cutting travel times to Mars and the outer planets 15 . NASA's Artemis program remains the cornerstone of U.S. lunar ambitions, targeting a sustained human presence on the Moon as a stepping stone to Mars — anchoring long-duration commercial contracts for landers, rovers, power systems, and habitats 16 . SpaceX's Starship — described as the most powerful rocket ever built — is the critical vehicle for both lunar and Mars missions, with upgraded Starlink satellite deployments planned for mid-2027 as an early commercial use case 17 . However, the investment profile of space exploration remains structurally complex. A significant share of exploration revenue is tied to U.S. federal appropriations, which are subject to political and fiscal pressures 18 . While emerging areas such as space tourism, in-space resource extraction, and space-based energy generation offer potentially transformative upside, they remain longer-dated opportunities with considerable execution risk. 19 Deep Space: The Technology Flywheel Behind Space Exploration Commercial Space Travel: Ambitions Continue to Advance The commercial space travel investment case appears compelling on a long-duration horizon — anchored by cost deflation, infrastructure buildout, and landmark IPO catalysts. Early commercial activity is beginning to take shape. Virgin Galactic is targeting the launch of its commercial spaceflight operations in 2026, initially focused on research payloads and private astronaut missions 20 . At the same time, commercial space launches have grown from 11 in 2016 to 157 in 2024, underscoring the impact of reusable rocket technologies in lowering the cost of access to space 21 . Ambitions for deep-space travel continue to advance. SpaceX has announced its first human spaceflight mission to Mars, a two-year Starship mission that will conduct a Mars fly-by, marking a concrete step toward interplanetary commercial travel 22 . Vast and Axiom Space, both developing commercial successors to the International Space Station, are expanding into Europe as NASA signals it may no longer fund development of multiple future stations in Earth's orbit. This shift is creating an opportunity for private operators to capture a larger share of orbital infrastructure and services 23 . Capital formation across the ecosystem is beginning to reflect this transition. Recent investments—including a $100 million commitment to Gemini Space Station —underscore growing private-sector interest in commercial orbital platforms and the broader low Earth orbit (LEO) economy 24 . At the same time, the commercial potential of human spaceflight and on-orbit servicing remains in an early stage of development 25 . Progress will depend on continued advancements in cost, cadence, and reliability of human-rated launch systems , alongside the buildout of supporting infrastructure. Commercial Space Travel: Compelling on a Long-Duration Horizon Space Mining: Near-Term Investable Exposure is Largely Indirect Space mining — encompassing asteroid mining and lunar resource extraction — is transitioning from science fiction to a nascent commercial and policy priority, underpinned by critical mineral scarcity on Earth, falling launch costs, and accelerating lunar infrastructure investment 26 . In the near-term, water extraction from lunar ice or near-Earth asteroids is the most immediate economic driver. Water may potentially be split into liquid hydrogen and oxygen to create rocket propellant, effectively establishing "gas stations" in space 27 . This emerging ecosystem is closely tied to broader government-led initiatives , which continue to anchor early-stage demand for lunar infrastructure and resource development. For example, Firefly Aerospace was awarded a $75 million subcontract by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory to deliver four drones to the Moon’s south pole in support of the MoonFall mission, targeted for no earlier than 2028 28 . From a functional perspective, mining lunar or near-Earth resources enables space agencies to build habitats and refuel spacecraft using locally sourced materials , reducing reliance on transporting inputs from Earth’s deep gravity well. Technological development remains a critical enabling factor. Given communication delays and the hazardous nature of extraterrestrial environments, mining operations will rely heavily on fully autonomous AI systems and advanced robotics . The strategic case for space mining is increasingly reinforced by terrestrial supply chain constraints. AI infrastructure relies on minerals like copper, lithium, and rare earths — resource-rich countries are increasingly imposing extraction taxes and supply controls, creating fiscal and geopolitical pressure across the AI supply chain and reinforcing the strategic case for alternative sourcing 29 . Commercial asteroid mining at scale remains a decade or more away — near-term investable exposure is largely indirect, through launch providers, rover manufacturers, and lunar infrastructure contractors 30 . Two Pillars of Space Mining: Asteroid Mining and Lunar Resource Extraction Space-Based Infrastructure: Transitioning to a Commercially-Driven Data-Focused Sector Space-based infrastructure — encompassing satellite constellations, orbital data centers, space-based power grids, in-orbit manufacturing, and spaceport facilities — is transitioning from a government-led domain to a commercially driven, data-focused sector, with private investment increasingly influencing its growth trajectory 31 . Technology firms are exploring orbital data infrastructure, while aerospace companies are scaling manufacturing capacity to support higher launch cadence and payload complexity. U.S. lawmakers are weighing legislation to boost the data center energy buildout, with space-based power cited as a potential long-term solution to the energy intensity of AI compute — underscoring the convergence of the AI infrastructure and space infrastructure investment themes 32 . At the same time, defense-related infrastructure remains a key anchor of near-term demand. Beyond defense, policymakers are increasingly linking space infrastructure to broader industrial and technological competitiveness. A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers introduced a bill in May 2026 to make property and infrastructure for space-based semiconductor manufacturing explicitly eligible for an investment tax credit — framing space manufacturing competitiveness as a national security issue vis-à-vis China 33 . Ultimately, space-based infrastructure is evolving from a government-funded capability into a commercially scalable platform, but its long-term investment profile will depend on the successful resolution of key economic and technical bottlenecks. Six Elements of Space-Based Infrastructure Conclusion The space economy reflects a classic infrastructure-led innovation cycle , characterized by significant upfront capital investment, uneven monetization timelines, and evolving competitive dynamics. While advancements in launch technology and satellite deployment have materially reduced the cost of accessing space, the next phase of value creation is increasingly dependent on the ability to monetize data, scale services, and establish sustainable commercial models . Space X’s addition to the Nasdaq-100 marked a significant milestone for the space economy’s representation within the index and highlights its growing relevance as a long-term thematic driver. SpaceX represents notable weight in the Nasdaq-100, providing the index with increased exposure to developments in the space economy. Through its exposure to companies involved in cloud computing, AI, semiconductors and satellite-enabled services, the Nasdaq-100 gives investors meaningful exposure to the space economy’s long term growth opportunities. In this context, investment opportunities are likely to diverge across the value chain. Near-term visibility remains strongest in infrastructure and data-driven segments , where demand is supported by defense spending, connectivity needs, and AI integration. By contrast, areas such as space mining, human spaceflight, and in-orbit manufacturing remain long-duration opportunities , with commercialization contingent on technological breakthroughs, regulatory clarity, and continued capital support. As a result, the opportunity is best viewed through a multi-decade lens , where value creation will depend on identifying the segments and business models most likely to translate technological title: Cybersecurity's Next Phase: Competing Business Models in a Growing Market
author: Ilaria Sangalli
description: July highlighted the growing divergence within the technology sector. While the Nasdaq-100® (NDX®) and the S&P Technology Select Sector Index declined 6.6% and 8.0%, respectively, broader equity markets proved more resilient, with the MSCI World Index gaining 0.5% and the S&P 500 ending the month roughly flat. Against this backdrop, the ISE Cyber Security UCITS™ Index (HUR™) declined 1.8% during the month, demonstrating relative resilience compared with broader technology benchmarks. The relative resilience of cybersecurity stocks suggests investors continue to view security spending as a strategic priority rather than a discretionary expense. Importantly, AI adoption appears to be creating additional demand for cybersecurity solutions rather than displacing existing security budgets, as organizations seek to protect AI models, sensitive data and increasingly complex digital environments. As a result, cybersecurity is emerging as a key beneficiary of the broader AI investment cycle. Recent comments from IBM support this view, indicating that enterprise customers continue to prioritize cybersecurity spending even as they accelerate investments in AI.
content: July highlighted the growing divergence within the technology sector. While the Nasdaq-100® (NDX®) and the S&P Technology Select Sector Index declined 6.6% and 8.0%, respectively, broader equity markets proved more resilient, with the MSCI World Index gaining 0.5% and the S&P 500 ending the month roughly flat. Against this backdrop, the Nasdaq CTA Cybersecurity Index™ Index (NQCYBR™) gained 2.18% during the month, demonstrating relative resilience compared with broader technology benchmarks. 1 The relative resilience of cybersecurity stocks may indicate continued market confidence in security spending, while recent IBM commentary suggests enterprise customers continue to prioritize cybersecurity spending alongside AI investments. 2 Importantly, AI adoption appears to be creating additional demand for cybersecurity solutions rather than displacing existing security budgets, as organizations seek to protect AI models, sensitive data and increasingly complex digital environments. As a result, cybersecurity appears to be a key beneficiary of the broader AI investment cycle. Cybersecurity’s Competitive Landscape: Platforms, Infrastructure and Specialists While the demand outlook for cybersecurity remains robust, competitive dynamics across the industry continue to evolve. The market is no longer defined only by specialist cybersecurity vendors competing against one another. Increasingly, cybersecurity is being embedded into the broader cloud, networking, software and infrastructure platforms that enterprises already use. This evolving landscape is particularly relevant for the NQCYBR Index, which provides exposure to a broad range of companies participating across the cybersecurity ecosystem. Importantly, NQCYBR is not limited to a single cybersecurity business model. The index includes: established cybersecurity vendors such as CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet; technology and infrastructure providers with meaningful cybersecurity businesses, including Cisco, Broadcom, Akamai and Cloudflare; more specialized cybersecurity companies such as Okta, Rubrik, and Qualys. This diversified exposure provides a useful lens through which to examine how the cybersecurity industry is evolving and where value creation is occurring across the ecosystem. Historically, enterprises purchased cybersecurity solutions from specialist vendors focused on specific areas such as endpoint protection, firewalls, identity management, vulnerability management, data protection and threat detection. These companies built their competitive advantage on dedicated security expertise, threat intelligence and rapid product innovation. That remains an important part of the market today, but the competitive landscape is evolving. Cybersecurity is increasingly moving from a collection of standalone point solutions toward broader platforms that aim to protect multiple layers of the enterprise technology stack. Several factors are driving this shift. As cyber threats become more sophisticated and enterprise IT environments grow increasingly complex, organizations are seeking to reduce operational complexity, consolidate vendors and improve visibility across their security environments. This has led to growing demand for integrated platforms that combine multiple security capabilities within a single ecosystem. While best-of-breed solutions continue to play an important role in many security architectures, the broader industry trend has been toward platform consolidation. Among the largest pure-play cybersecurity companies, this is increasingly reflected in product strategies that extend well beyond their original areas of specialization. 3 CrowdStrike has evolved from an endpoint security provider into a broader cybersecurity platform company, expanding its offerings across identity security, cloud security, next-generation SIEM, exposure management, threat intelligence and security operations. 4 In its most recent quarter, reported in June 2026, CrowdStrike generated $5.5 billion in annual recurring revenue, up 24% year over year, while record net new ARR reflected continued customer adoption of the Falcon platform. Momentum was particularly evident in Falcon Flex, CrowdStrike's flexible platform subscription model, with more than 300 accounts added during the quarter. Customers using Falcon Flex collectively represented over $1.9 billion in ending ARR, an increase of 99% year over year, reflecting increasing demand for integrated security platforms that can address multiple cybersecurity needs within a single ecosystem. 5 Palo Alto Networks has also been executing its own platformization strategy, encouraging customers to consolidate security spending across its network security, cloud security and security operations platforms. In its most recent reported quarter 6 , the company reported $8.13 billion in Next-Generation Security (NGS) ARR, representing 60% ARR growth, while management highlighted continued momentum in platformization. The company added approximately 110 net new platformization customers during the quarter, bringing the total to roughly 2,280. These customers represent deeper architectural commitments rather than individual product purchases and have historically exhibited stronger retention and expansion rates. Management also noted that the growing adoption of AI is increasing cybersecurity requirements across enterprise environments, reinforcing demand for integrated security platforms that can provide broader visibility and operational simplicity. 7 Fortinet is pursuing a similar platform-centric strategy, built around its FortiOS operating system, which enables customers to deploy networking and security capabilities across on-premises, cloud and hybrid environments through a unified architecture. This momentum was reflected in the company's Q1 results, with total billings increasing 31% to $2.09 billion, driven by broad-based strength across Secure Networking and Unified SASE. 8 At the same time, infrastructure and networking providers are increasingly embedding cybersecurity into broader enterprise platforms. Cisco has evolved beyond its networking heritage into a broader security platform provider. The company now offers solutions spanning secure access, XDR, AI security and zero-trust architecture, while recent initiatives focused on securing AI infrastructure and AI agents highlight how networking and cybersecurity are becoming increasingly interconnected. Cisco's strategy reflects a growing industry focus on integrating security capabilities directly into enterprise infrastructure and network architectures. An example of this approach is Cisco's Secure AI Factory with Nvidia, which aims to embed security across AI infrastructure deployments. 9 Broadcom participates in cybersecurity through the Symantec enterprise security portfolio, which provides endpoint, network, information and email security solutions across on-premises, cloud and hybrid environments. 10 Akamai illustrates how infrastructure providers are embedding cybersecurity into broader enterprise platforms. While the company built its business around content delivery and edge infrastructure, it has expanded into security through offerings such as web application protection, zero-trust access and microsegmentation. The launch of the Akamai Guardicore Platform further reflects the company's strategy of bringing multiple security functions together within a broader infrastructure platform. 11 However, the cybersecurity industry should not be viewed solely as a competition between large security platforms and infrastructure-led providers. A third group remains highly relevant: specialized cybersecurity vendors focused on specific, mission-critical security functions. These companies may not offer the broadest platforms, but they can remain strategically important where enterprises require deep domain expertise. Examples within NQCYBR include Okta in identity security, Rubrik in cyber resilience and recovery, and Qualys in vulnerability and risk management. Okta, for example, continues to position itself as an independent identity provider, with Q1 revenue of $765 million, up 11% year over year, and remaining performance obligations (RPO) of $4.719 billion, up 16% year over year. Management highlighted that AI agents are creating a new wave of identities that need to be secured and governed alongside human users. 12 Rubrik provides another example of a specialist vendor benefiting from a distinct cybersecurity need: cyber resilience. As ransomware and data breaches increase the importance of recovery, backup and business continuity, Rubrik has positioned itself around helping enterprises recover from cyber incidents. In its latest quarterly results, the company reported subscription ARR of $1.57 billion, up 32% year over year, while total revenue increased 39% year over year to $387.1 million. Management highlighted growing demand for cyber resilience across data, identity, and AI environments, describing Rubrik as an increasingly strategic platform for ‘agentic cyber resilience’. 13 Qualys, meanwhile, remains focused on vulnerability management, compliance and pre-breach risk management. In Q1, Qualys reported revenue of $175.6 million, up 10% year over year, with GAAP operating margin of 35% and non-GAAP operating margin of 46%. The company's profitability highlights how specialist providers can continue to create value in areas where customers prioritize deep expertise and established workflows, despite ongoing industry consolidation. 14 Source: FactSet. Price Performance as of July 31, 2026 Recent performance trends across NQCYBR constituents reinforce the view that cybersecurity is unlikely to evolve into a simple winner-takes-all market. Performance leadership has not been concentrated in any single business model. Broad cybersecurity platforms such as Fortinet, Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike have delivered strong gains, reflecting continued demand for integrated security offerings. At the same time, specialist providers such as Okta, as well as infrastructure and software companies including Fastly, Datadog and F5, have also ranked among the stronger performers. By contrast, returns have been more mixed for other constituents, including Check Point, OpenText and Zscaler. Taken together, these performance patterns suggest that value creation is occurring across multiple areas of the cybersecurity market. While platformization remains an important trend, enterprise spending continues to support a diverse set of business models, including integrated security platforms, infrastructure-led providers and specialist vendors. For market participants evaluating cybersecurity index exposure, this diversification may be relevant. The index provides exposure across these segments, rather than making a narrow bet on a single approach to cybersecurity. title: Institutional Investing 101: Who the Players Are and How Capital Really Moves
author: Nasdaq Capital Access Platforms
description: Learn what institutional investing is, how capital moves from asset owners to asset managers, and why fiduciary duty, governance, and manager selection shape institutional investment decisions.
content: Key Takeaways Institutional investors collectively manage trillions in global assets on behalf of beneficiaries ranging from individual retirees to entire national populations. The institutional ecosystem operates through two distinct roles: asset owners, who hold capital and set investment mandates, and asset managers, who execute strategies on their behalf. Many institutional investment decision are governed by fiduciary duty, which may include a legal obligation to act solely in the best interests of beneficiaries. Unlike retail investors, institutional investors usually operate on multi-decade or perpetual time horizons to meet obligations decades in the future. Capital allocation decisions pass through investment committees, boards, and often external consultants before reaching markets, a structure designed to protect beneficiaries. Manager selection involves rigorous quantitative and qualitative analysis, and the relationship continues through ongoing performance monitoring, compliance review, and periodic re-evaluation. Institutional investors represent more than US$70 trillion in investable assets globally , giving them significant influence over capital markets. Despite this scale, many professionals entering the space don’t fully understand how institutional capital moves, who makes the decisions, what governs them, and why the process looks so different from retail investing. Whether working in asset management, market infrastructure, or product marketing, professionals in these roles need a clear mental map of the institutional ecosystem. Otherwise, the terminology may become confusing, timelines may see arbitrary, and governance structures can be hard to understand. Understanding the institutional ecosystem requires knowing the key players, from pension funds and sovereign wealth funds to the asset managers they appoint and the consultants who advise them. It also calls for knowing how capital flows through the system, what governs the decisions at each stage, and what makes institutional investing so different from the retail context most professionals understand. What Is Institutional Investing? Institutional investing refers to the management of large pools of capital by organizations on behalf of beneficiaries or stakeholders. These organizations pool capital and invest at volumes that individual investors cannot access. There are several types of institutional investors in the landscape. Pension funds invest retirement assets on behalf of plan participants, and university and charitable endowments invest to fund ongoing operations and perpetual missions. Insurance companies invest policyholders' premium income to meet future claims, while sovereign wealth funds manage national reserves on behalf of entire populations. In each case, the capital belongs to someone else. The point of distinction in its institutional world (managing money for others) defines the principle of fiduciary duty , which means the institution is legally obligated to act solely in the beneficiaries' interests. Understanding the Institutional Difference For professionals new to this space, the institutional world can at first seem confusing, with mandates, governance structures, and an environment different from retail investing. However, the layers of governance are designed to protect beneficiaries, and understanding this is the foundation for everything else in the institutional ecosystem. Who Are the Key Players in Institutional Investing? There are several player types in the institutional landscape , each with its own source of capital, set of beneficiaries, and investment objective. Asset Owners: The Capital Holders Asset owners are the institutions that hold capital for others and are responsible for how it is invested. There are four main types: Pension Funds manage retirement assets on behalf of plan participants, investing to meet future benefit obligations. They operate across two structures: defined benefit plans and defined contribution plans. Endowments and Foundations manage capital for universities, hospitals, and charitable organizations Sovereign Wealth Funds are state-owned investment vehicles managing national reserves, often with decades-long investment horizons set up to preserve resource wealth for future generations. Insurance Companies invest premium income to meet future policyholder claims with a strategy shaped by the duration of liabilities. Asset Managers: The Investment Executors Asset managers are the firms hired by asset owners to execute investment strategies on their behalf. They range from large, diversified global managers to specialized boutiques focused on a single asset class or strategy. They are selected through competitive due diligence processes that evaluate the investment process, team, risk management, and alignment with mandate requirements. How Capital Flows Through the Institutional Investment System Institutional capital flows through a structured chain of governance, documentation, and oversight designed to protect beneficiaries at every stage. Understanding this chain can help explain how decisions are made and why they take time. The Decision Chain The process usually starts with a formal Investment Policy Statement , which defines objectives, risk parameters, asset allocation ranges, and performance benchmarks. After the policy is set, the asset owner issues mandates to asset managers: formal agreements that specify investment guidelines, benchmarks, fee structures, and reporting requirements. Asset managers then execute strategies within those mandate parameters and report performance back to the asset owner. Custodians and administrators handle settlement, safekeeping, and independent accounting, which adds another layer of verification at the point of execution. The Role of Investment Consultants Most asset owners use a consultant in this process. The consultant acts as an intermediary with an advisory capacity with advice on asset allocation, manager selection, portfolio construction, and performance monitoring. More than 85% of US institutional asset owners use investment consultants for help with manager selection, performance monitoring, and asset allocation. This layered structure explains why institutional capital often moves deliberately, as each decision passes through multiple checkpoints before reaching markets. What Makes Institutional Investing Different from Retail Investing? While retail investing and institutional investing operate in the same markets, they have different rules of scale, time, and accountability. Scale and Time Horizon Institutional portfolios aren’t construed to serve a single individual but thousands or millions of beneficiaries. As a result, investment decisions operate on a different scale, with large asset size, long-term investment horizons, regulatory constraints, and a governance framework. Many institutions also operate on time horizons ranging from 30 years for pension funds to perpetuity for endowments. Governance and Fiduciary Duty Where a retail investor makes personal decisions about their own capital, institutional decisions are governed by formal structures and a legal obligation to others. The institutions have a fiduciary duty to act solely in the beneficiaries' best interests it shapes every decision, from asset allocation to manager selection. Decisions are driven by investment committees, and evaluating an investment manager is a complex and detailed process of operational due diligence , governance assessment, and compliance review, often conducted over several months. Institutional investors also face regulatory and stakeholder reporting obligations to regulators, boards, and beneficiaries that have no equivalent in retail contexts. These differences mean that professionals supporting institutional clients must understand longer timelines, formal processes, and the weight of fiduciary responsibility.
